THE ARTS VS DIPLOMACY

By: Matuba Mahlatjie | Commission

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
When Politics Divides, the Arts Unite: U.S. Orchestra Bridges the Gap with South Africa

Unique Selling Point:
On the very day Donald Trump meets with South Africa’s president, a meeting overshadowed by years of strained relations, misinformation, and diplomatic tension, the University of Michigan Symphony Orchestra will take the stage in Pretoria. This tour features South African soprano Goitsemang Lehobye, a Michigan PhD graduate who embodies the circular exchange of talent between our countries. Lehobye herself embodies this tension. A South African artist thriving in the U.S. at a time when migrants face increasing hostility, she now returns home, not as a victim of her country, but as proof of its talent.

Summary:
While U.S.-SA relations face strain, from asylum claims based on debunked "white genocide" myths to trade tensions, the University of Michigan Symphony Orchestra is quietly bridging the divide.

Further information:
Timely News Hook: The Trump meeting gives urgency—this isn’t just a cultural feature, it’s a political moment.
Character-Driven: Goitsemang’s journey personalises the migrant/artist struggle.
Provocative Question to sharpen the political edge while keeping the arts at the heart: Who’s really shaping the future of U.S.-SA relations—politicians or artists?

Script:


(News Reporter 1) President Trump is meeting with the president…



(News Reporter 2) Crucial talks in Washington…



(News Reporter 3) Extraordinary meeting at the White House.



(Donald Trump) Death, death, horrible death. These are all white farmers who are being murdered.



(News Reporter 4) President Trump…



(Donald Trump) He asks about a jet that was….



(Cyril Ramaphosa) Through growing the economy, we’re then able to create more jobs. Because crime really thrives where there is inequality and unemployment.



(Masa Kekana) In the same week President Cyril Ramaphosa stood in Washington D.C., negotiating the threads of a fractured relationship, here in Pretoria, an American export of another kind took the stage. No treaties, no tariffs. Music.



(Masa Kekana) At the heart of this collaboration is Goitsemang Lehobye, a soprano with a PhD from the University of Michigan, who joins a growing wave of South African artists redefining classical music on global stages.



(Goitsemang Lehobye) Goitsemang is a girl from the dusty streets of Ga-Rankuwa. I loved music from a young age because I come from a very musical family.



(Masa Kekana) The South African-born singer has been living, studying and now working in the US for nearly ten years.



(Goitsemang Lehobye) I wanted to be an accountant. But then, as I saw people that looked like me doing what I do - seeing Ma’m Sibongile Khumalo, Virginia Davids and Loveline Madumo - made me believe that I could do it.



(Masa Kekana) Goitsemang’s journey, from township choirs to the world’s grandest stages, isn’t just talent. It’s defiance.



(Goitsemang Lehobye) It’s possible. But it’s possible through perseverance and hard work. It just doesn’t come to you, you know?



(Masa Kekana) The University of Pretoria, through tour organisers Classical Movements, became a natural choice to host this historic collaboration.



(Zamile Mzizi) The University of Pretoria’s Aula, at some time in this country's history, had to serve as the State Theatre. We've actually had many operas staged here. Many, many productions and a lot of South African musical legends were staging shows here.



(Masa Kekana) Zamile Mzizi, the University of Pretoria’s Symphony Orchestra Manager, says it’s fitting that the venue is hosting the American artists given its historical significance.



(Zamile Mzizi) If you look at it now, the post-millennials, etcetera… It is significant because people like you and me, who were not allowed to come and watch productions in places like this. But now we are studying here, we are working here and we are staging the productions that are happening in what used to be the State Theatre in a very different time of our history.



(Masa Kekana) In 1895, acclaimed South African composer, journalist and clergyman John Knox Bokwe wrote one of Africa’s first notated lament - a hymn pleading for freedom from colonial chains.



(Masa Kekana) Today, as misinformation fuels division and wars burn borders, his notes still weep.



(Donald Trump) We are making it as easy as possible for illegal aliens to leave America.



(Donald Trump) My administration has launched the most sweeping border and immigration crackdown in American history. We will make America wealthy again.



(Masa Kekana) Right now, the talk of the globe; the shift in geopolitics, a growing anti-migrant rhetoric… What’s your experience been like in this area in particular?



(Goitsemang Lehobye) It’s been a little difficult just with things being a little weird and being unsure. At some point, we were sitting down with my teacher and conductor, thinking about should I go to South Africa. Because if I go, if I go out of the country, would they let me back in?



(Masa Kekana) Leading this transatlantic collaboration is Maestro Kenneth Kiesler, Grammy-nominated conductor, mentor to generations and a global force in classical music.



(Masa Kekana) Speaking about nation-building songs; was that also deliberate when we're looking at the political climate that we find ourselves in? The strained relations between South Africa and the US currently?



(Kenneth Kiesler) Well, when I did this programming, there were no strained relations that I was aware of at the time. So, it's not a response to that. I'm glad we're doing them now.



(Masa Kekana) Kiesler’s work in Pretoria cements his belief that talent knows no borders, a philosophy as timely as political headlines between South Africa and the United States.



(Kenneth Kiesler) At the time, I wanted to know which music is known and means something to people and has a history and resonates with people. And now it's beginning to resonate with us as well. We've dug in. Those of us who didn't know the music before, what do the words mean and why did people sing these things. Bawo Thixo Somanadla, for example.



(Male 1) Can we say “sigqibana”, “sigqibana”? The q-click is actually the easiest of all the Xhosa clicks. Q-q-q-q-q-q. This song is about “Why, oh Lord, are we in this mess? And why are we finishing each other?” Khuteni sigqibana nje? Nhe? Ndisoloko ndisithi mayidlule lendebe. “Let this too pass”.



(Masa Kekana) An orchestra that sings? In isiXhosa - a language they were introduced to in just a few hours? It’s more than a performance, it’s respect.



(Donald Trump) I don’t know where you got my number, but I picked up. He said, “I want to come over and see you.” That was my honour. Thank you very much for being here.



(Cyril Ramaphosa) You’re most welcome.



(Masa Kekana) In Washington, headlines focused on what wasn’t achieved. But in Pretoria? We heard what’s possible when the world plays in unison.



(Zamile Mzizi) What we come to do on this stage is not to talk politics. Politics tends to sometimes forget the people down there who are living with the consequences of the politics. And what music does, it just helps us all reconnect from a heart level. Because we're not discussing policies and we're not discussing economics. Maybe we can say we are commenting about it in the music we are performing. But what we are doing here is connecting on an emotional level. Musicians, artists all over the world - we are like-minded people.



(Masa Kekana) Like-minded people with collaboration that proves that when politics fail, art builds. Not walls - bridges.



(Goitsemang Lehobye) The love for what I do, the feelings I got from what I do, helped me, pushed me to keep trying. And I believed, since it chose me, I needed to do something with it. Which I believe I was sent here to sing so that I can uplift people. I can heal people, you know? I can send out messages that I normally wouldn't have had the platform to do.



(Masa Kekana) Talks ended without applause in Washington D.C., a script of division, unworthy of the stage. But here in Pretoria, under a shared symphony of hope, an audience rose not for politicians, but for a truth louder than lies. Harmony triumphs where discord fails.
